Desire of Women
de-ZIRE of WIM-en
noun phrase
A phrase rendering the Hebrew chemdath nashim — chemdah, that which is desired or precious, and nashim, women. It occurs once, in Daniel’s prophecy of the wilful king, and its exact reference has been debated since the earliest commentators.

Biblical Definition

The phrase belongs to Daniel’s portrait of the king who does according to his will: “Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all” (Dan 11:37). The structure of the verse is the key to it. Three things are named that the king disregards, and the outer two are plainly religious — the God of his fathers and any god — with the phrase sitting between them. That placement has led most sober interpreters to take the desire of women as a deity or object of devotion rather than a comment on the king’s domestic life: either a god particularly adored by women, such as Tammuz, whom Ezekiel saw women weeping for at the gate of the LORD’s house, or the hope of Hebrew women to bear the Messiah. Others take it simply of natural affection, a man so consumed by self-exaltation that he has no room for ordinary human love. What is beyond dispute is the verse’s conclusion, which the whole sentence drives toward: he shall magnify himself above all. Whatever the phrase names, it is one more thing sacrificed to self-magnification, and Daniel’s wilful king is recognisable in every age — a man who will give up his God, his gods, and his affections rather than give up himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

A phrase in Daniel’s prophecy of the wilful king, denoting something he disregards — most probably an object of devotion, and set between two plainly religious terms.

expand to see more

DESIRE, n. That which is desired; the object of longing.

Rendering the Hebrew chemdah, a precious or desirable thing.

The phrase the desire of women occurs only at Dan 11:37.

Anciently understood by many of a deity peculiarly honoured by women, as Tammuz (Eze 8:14).

By others, of the hope of Hebrew women to be mother of the promised seed.

Key Scripture

Dan 11:36 — "And the king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvellous things against the God of gods, and shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done."

Dan 11:37 — "Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all."

Eze 8:14 — "Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the LORD'S house which was toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz."

2Th 2:4 — "Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God."

Modern Corruption

Obscure prophetic phrases are routinely turned into confident charts of current events, and this one has carried a long train of speculation about the identity and habits of Antichrist.

expand to see more

The corruption is speculative prophecy. A phrase occurring once, whose reference the ancient commentators already disputed, has been made to yield detailed conclusions about the personal life, nationality, and religion of a coming Antichrist, and each generation’s identification has aged badly. The dictionary rejects the whole method. Scripture’s obscure places are to be read in the light of its plain places, not the reverse, and a doctrine erected on a disputed clause is a house built on the one stone in the wall no one can identify. Where the Reformers and the Puritans read Dan 11 they were far more concerned with the character it describes than with dating its fulfilment.

Recover the plain sense: the verse is not obscure about its main assertion. He shall magnify himself above all — that is the wilful king’s defining act, and Paul describes the same figure in terms that leave nothing to guess: he opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped (2Th 2:4). What Daniel gives us is a portrait of self-exaltation so complete that it discards inherited religion, foreign religion, and human affection alike, keeping nothing that might rival the self. That description is useful to every reader now, whatever the phrase in the middle means, because the spirit it describes is not confined to one man at the end of history. Every soul knows something of the impulse to keep the self at the centre, and the antidote is the mind that was in Christ Jesus, who being in the form of God made Himself of no reputation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chemdath nashim, the desire of women — a disputed phrase in Dan 11:37, framed by two religious terms and driving to self-magnification.

expand to see more

Desire of women — Hebrew chemdath nashim, from chemdah, a desirable thing.

Occurs only at Dan 11:37, in the prophecy of the wilful king.

Set between the God of his fathers and any god — both plainly religious terms.

Anciently referred by many to Tammuz, wept for by women in Eze 8:14.

By others to the hope of Hebrew women to bear the promised seed.

Usage

"Read the phrase by its frame: the outer two terms are objects of worship."

"The verse’s undisputed point is he shall magnify himself above all."

"2Th 2:4 describes the same self-exalting figure in plain terms."
